items.q: A 55-year-old patient exhibits right-sided hemiparesis with spastic tone, hyperreflexia, and sustained ankle clonus. Plantar reflex on the right shows an extensor Babinski response. Muscle fasciculations are completely absent. These findings are characteristic of which type of lesion?
items.exp: Upper motor neuron lesions feature spastic tone (clasp-knife), hyperreflexia, clonus, and positive extensor Babinski response due to loss of descending corticospinal inhibition.
r: Correct. Hyperreflexia, spasticity, clonus, and Babinski sign are cardinal UMN signs.
Incorrect. LMN lesions produce hypotonia, hyporeflexia, wasting, and fasciculations.
Incorrect. Neuromuscular junction disorders produce fatigable weakness without tone/reflex changes.
Incorrect. Myopathies cause symmetric proximal weakness with preserved reflexes initially.
items.kp: Upper motor neuron lesions manifest with spasticity, hyperreflexia, ankle clonus, and positive extensor Babinski signs.

items.q: A patient presents with right-sided oculomotor nerve palsy (ptosis, dilated pupil, eye resting 'down and out') accompanied by contralateral (left-sided) spastic hemiparesis of the face, arm, and leg. What is the anatomical diagnosis?
items.exp: Weber syndrome is an alternating midbrain syndrome caused by occlusion of paramedian branches of PCA, damaging the exiting CN III fascicles and the adjacent cerebral peduncle (corticospinal tract).
r: Correct. Weber syndrome features ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiparesis.
Incorrect. Wallenberg syndrome damages lateral medulla with CN IX/X and sensory signs.
Incorrect. Millard-Gubler syndrome features CN VI/VII palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.
Incorrect. Dejerine syndrome features CN XII palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.
items.kp: Weber syndrome localizes to the midbrain, presenting with ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiplegia.

items.q: A 62-year-old patient presents with sudden severe vertigo, hoarseness, dysphagia, Horner syndrome on the right, ataxia on the right, loss of pain/temperature on the right side of the face, and loss of pain/temperature on the left side of the body. Which artery is occluded?
items.exp: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome results from PICA or vertebral artery occlusion. It damages nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia/hoarseness), spinal trigeminal tract (ipsilateral face numbness), and spinothalamic tract (contralateral body numbness).
r: Correct. Wallenberg syndrome is caused by PICA occlusion damaging lateral medulla.
Incorrect. AICA occlusion causes lateral pontine syndrome with facial nerve palsy and deafness.
Incorrect. Basilar artery causes locked-in state or bilateral pontine ischemia.
Incorrect. Superior cerebellar artery causes ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia without crossed sensory loss.
items.kp: Wallenberg lateral medullary syndrome results from PICA occlusion, causing dysphagia, hoarseness, Horner syndrome, and crossed analgesia.

items.q: According to the 'rule of four' for brainstem localization, which four cranial nerves emerge directly from the medulla oblongata?
o: CN IX, X, XI, and XII
CN V, VI, VII, and VIII
CN III, IV, VI, and XII
CN I, II, III, and IV
items.exp: The rule of four states that 4 cranial nerves emerge from the medulla: glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), accessory (XI), and hypoglossal (XII).
r: Correct. CN IX, X, XI, and XII exit from the medulla oblongata.
Incorrect. CN V, VI, VII, and VIII emerge from the pons.
Incorrect. CN III and IV exit from the midbrain.
Incorrect. CN I and II are forebrain structures.
items.kp: The medulla oblongata houses and gives exit to cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII.

items.q: A stroke patient presents with ipsilateral abducens (CN VI) palsy, ipsilateral facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, and contralateral hemiparesis. Where is the lesion located?
items.exp: Millard-Gubler syndrome is a ventral pontine alternating syndrome damaging exiting CN VI and VII fascicles along with the corticospinal tract.
r: Correct. Millard-Gubler syndrome involves ventral pons, affecting CN VI, VII, and corticospinal tract.
Incorrect. Weber involves midbrain CN III.
Incorrect. Wallenberg involves lateral medulla.
Incorrect. Dejerine involves medial medulla with CN XII.
items.kp: Millard-Gubler syndrome localizes to the ventral pons, causing ipsilateral CN VI and VII palsies with contralateral hemiparesis.

items.q: Which motor pathway structure crosses in the caudal medulla oblongata at the pyramidal decussation?
items.exp: At the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla, approximately 85% of descending corticospinal fibers cross the midline to form the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral funiculus of the spinal cord.
r: Correct. Corticospinal fibers cross at the medullary pyramidal decussation.
Incorrect. Spinocerebellar tracts ascend uncrossed or double-crossed.
Incorrect. MLF coordinates vestibular and ocular motor nuclei.
Incorrect. Rubrospinal tract decussates in the midbrain.
items.kp: Eighty-five percent of corticospinal fibers cross at the medullary pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract.

items.q: A patient presents with tongue deviation to the right side on protrusion, accompanied by left-sided hemiplegia sparing the face. Where is the vascular lesion?
o: Right medial medulla (anterior spinal artery branch)
items.exp: Dejerine (medial medullary) syndrome is caused by anterior spinal artery or paramedian vertebral occlusion, damaging the hypoglossal nucleus/nerve (tongue deviates to lesion side) and corticospinal tract.
r: Correct. Right medial medullary infarction damages right CN XII and uncrossed corticospinal fibers.
Incorrect. Lateral medulla spares CN XII and motor fibers.
Incorrect. Midbrain lesions involve CN III, not CN XII.
Incorrect. Internal capsule lesions produce contralateral face/arm/leg weakness without tongue atrophy.
items.kp: Medial medullary syndrome damages CN XII (tongue deviates towards lesion) and corticospinal tract (contralateral hemiparesis).

items.q: Brown-Sequard syndrome following a spinal cord hemisection produces which classic pattern of neurological deficits below the lesion level?
o: Ipsilateral motor weakness and vibration loss; contralateral pain and temperature loss
Bilateral motor weakness with preserved vibration sense
Contralateral motor weakness and ipsilateral pain/temperature loss
Bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved motor function
items.exp: Spinal cord hemisection damages the uncrossed corticospinal tract (ipsilateral weakness), uncrossed dorsal columns (ipsilateral touch/vibration loss), and crossed spinothalamic tract (contralateral pain/temperature loss).
r: Correct. Brown-Sequard produces ipsilateral weakness/vibration loss and contralateral pain/temperature loss.
Incorrect. Bilateral weakness suggests transverse myelitis or complete transection.
Incorrect. Motor weakness is strictly ipsilateral below the hemisection.
Incorrect. Sparing of motor with loss of pain suggests anterior cord syndrome.
items.kp: Brown-Sequard hemicord syndrome causes ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss with contralateral pain and temperature analgesia.

items.q: Which clinical feature definitively differentiates a peripheral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (Bell palsy) from a central upper motor neuron facial weakness?
o: Paralysis of forehead frontalis and orbicularis oculi muscles
Inability to smile on the affected side
items.exp: The forehead (frontalis muscle) receives bilateral upper motor neuron cortical innervation. An LMN facial palsy impairs the entire ipsilateral face including the forehead, whereas an UMN lesion spares the forehead.
r: Correct. Forehead weakness confirms LMN facial palsy; forehead sparing indicates a central UMN lesion.
Incorrect. Both UMN and LMN lesions impair voluntary smiling.
Incorrect. Nasolabial fold flattens in both UMN and LMN weakness.
Incorrect. Drooling occurs in both UMN and LMN weakness.
items.kp: Forehead involvement confirms a lower motor neuron facial palsy, whereas forehead sparing signifies a central upper motor neuron lesion.

items.q: A patient presents with bilateral symmetrical distal extremity sensory loss in a 'glove-and-stocking' distribution, loss of ankle jerk reflexes, and mild distal motor weakness. Where is the primary pathological process?
items.exp: Symmetric distal sensory loss in a glove-and-stocking distribution with absent distal reflexes is the hallmark of a length-dependent peripheral polyneuropathy.
r: Correct. Glove-and-stocking sensory impairment with lost ankle jerks defines length-dependent polyneuropathy.
Incorrect. Myelopathy presents with a sensory level and upper motor neuron signs.
Incorrect. Internal capsule infarcts produce unilateral hemiparesis.
Incorrect. Syrinx causes cape-like suspended dissociated sensory loss across upper extremities.
items.kp: Glove-and-stocking sensory loss coupled with absent ankle reflexes localizes to peripheral length-dependent polyneuropathy.
